Safe methods
GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are defined as safe methods. The client does not request a change in server state when it uses a safe method.
Idempotent methods
An idempotent method has the same intended effect when repeated as when executed once. PUT, DELETE and safe methods are idempotent. A client can sometimes retry after a dropped connection.
HEAD requests
HEAD has the same semantics as GET except the server sends no response content. It can retrieve representation metadata without transferring the body.
PUT requests
PUT asks the server to create or replace the state of the target resource with the supplied representation. A newly created resource normally receives 201.
If-Match
If-Match uses strong entity tag comparison. It can protect updates against overwriting changes made by another client, and a failed precondition normally produces status 412.
If-None-Match
If-None-Match is false when a listed entity tag matches the selected representation. A false condition on GET or HEAD can produce 304, while other methods normally receive 412.
304 Not Modified
Status code 304 tells the client that its cached representation is still valid after a conditional GET or HEAD. The representation is unmodified, so the response has no body.
401 Unauthorized
A 401 response indicates that the request lacks valid authentication credentials. The server sends a WWW-Authenticate challenge.
405 Method Not Allowed
405 means the server knows the method but the target resource does not support it. The response includes an Allow field with supported methods.
503 Service Unavailable
A server can use 503 for temporary overload or scheduled maintenance and may supply Retry-After to indicate how long to wait.
Freshness
A stored response is fresh while its age is below its freshness lifetime. A fresh response can generally be reused without first checking with the origin.
Cache validation
A cache can send a conditional request to validate a stored response. Validators such as an entity tag or modification date help the origin determine whether a cached representation can be reused.
Cache-Control max-age
The response max-age directive gives the number of seconds after generation when the response becomes stale.
Cache-Control no-store
The no-store response directive tells caches to avoid storing the request or response and to make a best effort to remove volatile copies promptly.
Cache-Control private
A response marked private can be stored by a private cache under the usual constraints. A shared cache must not store the full response when the directive is unqualified.
HTTP/1.1 message body length
Message framing determines how much content to read. A message with both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length can indicate request smuggling or response splitting and needs special handling.
Chunked transfer coding
Chunked transfer coding sends content as chunks prefixed with their size in hexadecimal. A final zero-size chunk ends the sequence, followed by any trailers.
HTTP request smuggling
Request smuggling exploits disagreements about message boundaries between recipients such as a proxy and an origin server. Strict parsing and consistent framing reduce the risk.
